Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The work took place beside the low timber bridge, where the path divides toward Hemlock Cut on the left and the creek overlook on the right. The crew put a new printed panel into the existing frame and left the wooden post in place. I was there as a volunteer trail monitor, not as a member of the crew, and I watched from the gravel turnout while they did the work. The replacement was a definite event, not a plan for a later visit. It was finished before the afternoon shuttle made its regular stop at the preserve entrance.

The old panel had been hard to read for several weeks. Rainwater had gotten under its clear surface film, and the lettering and arrow for the creek overlook were peeling and pale in that area. The problem was not that the fork had moved or that the route had been closed. Both paths still started at their usual places. The practical reason for replacing the panel was that a hiker approaching the fork could not reliably read the right-hand direction. The crew had looked at it on an earlier inspection, but I do not know the date of that inspection. I saw the damaged film and faded arrow myself on the previous Saturday, when I walked past on my usual check.

On Tuesday, parks coordinator Nora Bell left a note at the trail desk saying that the replacement panel was ready and that the crew would install it the following morning if the forecast stayed dry. The note also said the crew had printed the same two route names and distances as before. It did not say the sign was being changed because either trail had been rerouted. I asked Nora whether the sign would have a different arrow layout. She said, “No, the routes are the same; the right arrow just needs to be readable again.” That answer was useful to me because two visitors had asked about the fork during the month, and I had pointed them toward the small map on the kiosk instead of trying to interpret the damaged panel.

1. Work at the fork

I reached the turnout at about nine in the morning on Wednesday. Parks staff members Leon Price and Tessa Ward had already taken the old panel out of the frame and set it face up on a canvas sheet. They checked the frame for loose screws, and Leon tightened one screw at the lower corner. Neither of them removed the post. Tessa wiped the inside edges of the frame with a cloth, while Leon compared the new panel with a folded work sheet. I could not read the small print from where I stood, but I heard him name Hemlock Cut and the creek overlook as he checked the order. There was no conversation about changing the routes or adding another destination.

The new panel was a little cleaner in appearance than the old one, but its information was not different. The two trail names, the distance figures, and the arrows matched the wording and arrangement Nora had described. The right arrow was dark and easy to make out while the panel was on the canvas, though I did not test how it looked from the far side of the fork. Tessa held the panel while Leon fastened it into the frame. They took turns checking that it sat evenly along the edges, and then they wiped a thumbprint from the lower part of the surface. The work took less time than it had taken me to finish my notes from the morning check.

I asked Leon whether the crew had brought a spare panel in case the frame was damaged. He said they had one with them, but that the frame had held up and did not need to be replaced. The spare stayed in the vehicle. He explained that the new panel had been printed at the county shop from the sign file already on record, rather than drawn by hand at the trailhead. I did not see the file, and I cannot say when it was last updated. The crew kept the old panel on the canvas while they finished, then put it flat in the back of their vehicle. They did not leave it beside the path or put it in the waste bin at the turnout.

I felt relieved when the clear face of the new panel went into the frame. That is my personal reaction, and I may be giving a small sign too much importance because I spend time answering questions at this fork. I was not claiming that the sign had caused anyone to get lost. I had only heard the two questions and seen that the arrow was difficult to read. When I told Leon that I was glad the panel was being replaced, he replied, “It was due for attention; the post is still solid.” I took that as a comment about the condition of the sign, not a statement that the crew had documented a lost hiker or a safety incident.

After the panel was fitted, Leon stepped back onto the path leading from the bridge and looked at it from several paces away. Tessa stayed beside the frame and held the folded work sheet. They checked the words once more, then packed the cloth and tools into a small case. I watched them leave the fork and drive toward the service road, but I did not go with them. Their work sheet was not offered to me, so I do not know what was written in its other fields. Nora’s note had mentioned that the crew would return the old panel to the county depot, and the crew’s handling of it was consistent with that note; I did not see what happened after the vehicle left.

2. Notes from my check

I recorded the replacement in my volunteer log after the crew had gone. I wrote the date, the north fork location, the names of the two trail directions, and the fact that the existing post remained in place. I also noted that the new panel matched the listed distances and that its right arrow looked darker at close range. I did not write that either route was safer, easier, or more popular after the work, because I had not walked both routes that morning and did not compare visitor choices before and after. The log is kept in the trail desk drawer with the weekly condition sheets.

The afternoon shuttle passed the entrance while I was still at the turnout, and I finished checking the nearby bridge rail before leaving. The bridge rail had no loose boards when I pressed it by hand. That was a separate item on my routine check, not part of the sign work. I put the folded condition sheet back in the drawer when I returned to the desk, next to Nora’s note about the printed panel.
